George Washington's first inauguration. On April 30, 1789, in New York City, the nation's capital at the time, George Washington took the oath of office as the first president of the United States. Washington was the only president in American history to be unanimously elected by the Electoral College, receiving every elector's vote. Despite his reluctance to take power, viewing the position as a burden, he accepted it out of duty to preserve the newly formed nation. Approximately ten thousand people gathered to witness the ceremony on Wall Street, witnessing a moment that would set the tone for the presidency itself. Washington's inaugural address was relatively brief, emphasizing divine providence and warning against party factionalism at a time when political unity was fragile. Through his actions and conduct as president, Washington established many customs that would shape the office for generations. Most famously, he honored an unwritten tradition of two-term presidencies that would be respected by every president until Franklin Roosevelt. His measured leadership set precedents through dignified conduct and restraint that would define executive expectations for the nation's future.
